toc.title: What safety and safety cues are
Your safety cues are your own
Anchoring in safety brings the impulse to connect

blocks.p: I want to talk about feeling anchored in safety, the impulse to connect, and my newfound interest in design, which has helped me get more anchored in my own polyvagal safety state. My hope is that you get curious about what brings you into your own safety state that maybe you don't realize.

blocks.h: What safety and safety cues are

blocks.p: When I say safety, I'm referring to being anchored in the safe and social state of your autonomic nervous system. It's the polyvagal sense of the word safety.

A safety cue is something that triggers that safety state. It could be gentle touch. It could be gentle eye contact, a smell, a texture, all kinds of things. It could be when your favorite team wins, maybe, though that's more of a perception kind of thing.

Deb Dana put it simply when she was on the podcast: "There have to be more cues of safety than danger in order for me to move into ventral." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))
When you're in safety, some significant changes happen.

ul: Physical changes. Your breathing becomes easier, lighter. For myself and my therapy clients, when that state of safety is triggered, we can breathe easier into our belly. That's a pretty typical way of telling. You're able to smile. If you're not in your safety state, smiling becomes a lot more difficult, or it's just fake. There's less muscle tension and more relaxation. You can play with people. You can be close. You can hug.

An impulse to connect. Hugging and playing are part of this impulse to connect with others. It's absolutely fundamental to the state of safety. We don't choose to. We just have this impulse to connect.

Presence. We feel more in the present moment, more grounded in our body. We have more of an experience of our senses. We're taking it all in at once, but it's not overwhelming. There's just this settling into the experience of the present moment.
Cognitive changes. We can think critically. We can weigh pros and cons. We can plan things out and set realistic goals. We can understand people better. Our thoughts become more hopeful.
Emotional changes. We can feel happiness, connection, joy, excitement, love, all kinds of stuff. Hope, I think, is a big one too.

blocks.p: It's not just biology, and it's not just behavior. When that biology is active, the experience of the present moment changes. It's altered to be more connected. That's what's really central to the polyvagal state of safety.

Safety cues help you feel more grounded in the present moment, more safe, more connected, and they could be a whole bunch of things. For me, with scents, I'm usually pulled toward vanillas, cinnamons, wood kinds of scents. I also like citrus a lot. A safety cue could be a texture. It could be someone you care about giving you a hug.

Something I noticed recently is a major, major safety cue for me, something that really grounds me and helps me feel more in my body, more in the present moment: design, and specifically typography. Type, font, text, words. Designing them, sizing them, giving them white space, laying them out.

I think I've always kind of known I like it. I really respond to what my system finds to be pleasing typography. I always assumed I didn't have it within me to create my own. Things like graffiti have always pulled me in, seeing how people can bend and break letters and create art out of it. I've never been able to do it, not even with a marker, but there's an interest there. It's something I could have developed and flourished in, probably, but it just wasn't on my path.

It started off as general web design. I like to play around with my website and tweak things, so I started looking at what other people were doing. I liked how people laid things out, how creative they could get, what colors they used, and I realized there's a science behind this stuff. I started delving deeper into layouts, specifically with text, and looking at Behance, where people show off their designs.

I kept going down that rabbit hole, and I learned about something called Swiss design, and I fell head over heels in love with it. It spoke to me on a deep level: the visual layout of it, but also the mathematics of it, the logical structure of things. It was, and is, an instant click for me. Josef Müller-Brockmann is one of the pioneers of something called the Swiss grid. Very minimal. A lot of times black and white, though it doesn't have to be. I bought his book and some other books on typography and design, and I just feel fantastic.

It's very soothing, but very grounding. I can look at this stuff for hours. It can become mindless, but when I'm mindfully doing it, I feel very present, very inspired, very excited, and also very grounded. Things just make sense. The way my brain responded to it was this sense of clarity, and clarity is something I strive for in the way I speak and the way I create my courses. Clarity and structure are kind of a big deal for me.

blocks.h: Your safety cues are your own

blocks.p: In all honesty, Swiss design is probably pretty boring to other people. It can be very structured, very bland looking. But for me, it just works. It clicks.

All of our safety cues are different. What I find to be a safety cue in Swiss grid design may be boring as heck for you, or mind-numbing. It may even cause a neuroception of danger and make you flip the page and move on.

So safety can come in unexpected places. For me, it's this design thing. I think it was always kind of there, and I just didn't realize it. As I'm becoming more and more mindful of what helps me feel grounded, I realize this is one of those things.

blocks.h: Anchoring in safety brings the impulse to connect

blocks.p: Being more anchored in your safety state will trigger impulses within you to connect with others. I've found that for myself as I keep doing my own safety anchoring work, trying to develop my capacity to self-regulate and access my safety state more and more.

I've felt it with the podcast. I hadn't recorded something new in a couple of months, and as I've become more grounded, I feel this impulse to connect with you all over again. It's kind of odd, because a podcast is probably the least connected way of connecting. But for me it does feel like some sort of connection. I get something out of it, so I'm following that impulse.

I've also felt the impulse to connect with the people in my courses, and I kind of don't know how. I'm not a super social person. I'm actually pretty bad at it. I feel this impulse to build community, but I'm terrible at building community, probably because I've isolated, or been introverted, my entire life, and I still am. My social skills are not super high, in all honesty. So I just told them, "I'm not good at this connection stuff, but I want you to know I appreciate you."

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: I've also felt more of an impulse to connect with my family. I'm so proud of being a dad. It's extremely important in my life, and I think it's a strength of mine. But around that time, I noticed that I wanted to build a deeper relationship with my kids. It's always been there, but I feel it differently now. There's a shift happening within me that I'm noticing.

One night I picked my daughter up from her friend's house, where they'd done a Stranger Things marathon. It was late, and it was just her and me in the car. I realized her friends are these nerdy, awkward kids, and so is she, very much so. But they're good kids. She's picked good friends. And I felt proud of her, and I felt like I needed to express that.

I tell my kids I'm proud of them constantly. That's not the issue at all. But when you're in the car with someone, driving home late at night, it has a different feel to it. It has a different punch, a different impact. So I said something like, "Hey, I'm really proud of you. You've surrounded yourself with some good people, and you're pretty darn awesome yourself."

I've noticed myself telling my kids more often than I already was that I'm proud of them, that they're doing a good job, that I love them. I make an effort to say I love you to my kids every day, but I really don't want it to become routine. I want it to feel more raw, more genuine. I want there to be more of a connection and impact to it.

I've also noticed a bit more patience with everybody. I feel my capacity to receive support growing, and my capacity to give unconditional support growing. These aren't areas I felt I had a huge issue in, but seeing them grow, noticing it, and giving myself some kudos feels pretty good.

I've also had an impulse to grow myself as far as my accomplishments go, this whole business and entrepreneur kind of thing. At the time, I was working toward more private practice hours and fewer salaried job hours. I'm pushing myself to take on new challenges and build more independence, and it feels good. It feels like I'm on a path of growth, following these little impulses here and there, and it feels right. I feel proud of myself.

From all this, I'm noticing more belief in myself, and that feels pretty damn good. I feel more connected. I feel those impulses. They've been there, but kind of dormant, or isolated to my family. Now my ability to connect with other people, and to be okay with it, is growing. Again, I'm not a super social person. I do just fine on my own. But my capacity to connect with people and be okay with it keeps growing. It's not a good or bad thing. It's just growing.
